t.2.53.2: Then, having joined my palms in reverence to the two princes, I mounted the chariot and set out, bearing that sorrow all the while.
t.2.53.1: But as I turned back, my horses would not move along the road, shedding hot tears now that Rāma had set out for the forest.
t.2.53.3: Together with Guha, I stayed right there for many days, in the hope that Rāma might call me back again.
t.2.53.4: In your realm, O great king, even the trees, wasted by the calamity that has befallen Rāma, have withered, together with their flowers, shoots and buds.
t.2.53.5: The creatures did not stir, nor did the beasts of prey roam about; overcome by grief for Rāma, that forest fell silent.
t.2.53.6: And, O lord of men, the lotus pools have their lotus leaves withered and their waters turbid; their lotuses are scorched, and their fish and birds have hidden themselves away.
t.2.53.8: As I enter Ayodhyā, no one greets me; the people, not seeing Rāma, sigh again and again.
t.2.53.7: The flowers born in water and the garlands born on land, now faint in fragrance, and the fruits as well, do not shine today as they did before.
t.2.53.9: From mansions, palaces and lofty towers the women, wasted by not seeing Rāma, beheld the chariot returned and raised cries of grief.
t.2.53.10: With their long, clear eyes flooded by a rush of tears, the women, plainly more stricken with grief, gaze at one another.
t.2.53.11: Because of my distress, I perceive no difference at all between enemies and friends, or people who are indifferent.
t.2.53.13: O great king, joyless and stricken by Rāma's banishment, Ayodhyā appears to me like Kausalyā bereft of her son.
t.2.53.12: The city's people were joyless and its elephants and horses dejected; it lay withered amid cries of anguish, resounding with the sound of deep sighs.
t.2.53.14: Having heard the words of the charioteer, the king, in a voice most wretched and choked with tears, said this to that charioteer.
t.2.53.16: Without consulting my friends, my ministers, or the townsfolk, I did this deed rashly, out of infatuation, for the sake of a woman.
t.2.53.15: Directed by Kaikeyī, whose nature springs from a wicked lineage, I did not deliberate together with the elders skilled in counsel.
t.2.53.17: Surely, O Sūta, it is by the force of destiny, or else by mere chance, that this great calamity has come about for the destruction of this family.
t.2.53.18: O charioteer, if I have ever done any good deed for you, quickly bring me to Rāma, for my life-breaths are hastening me away.
t.2.53.20: Or else, the mighty-armed one will have gone far by now; then set me alone upon the chariot and quickly show me to Rāma.
t.2.53.19: Whatever command of mine there may be, let it bring Rāghava back; without Rāma I shall not be able to live even for a moment.
t.2.53.22: If I do not see Rāma, the red-eyed, mighty-armed one adorned with jeweled earrings, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
t.2.53.21: Where is that great archer with rounded teeth, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa? If I live, may I see him well, together with Sītā.
t.2.53.23: What could be more sorrowful than this, that I, having fallen into this state, do not see here Rāghava, the delight of the Ikṣvākus?
t.2.53.24: Alas Rāma, alas younger brother of Rāma, alas Vaidehī, poor ascetic lady! You do not know that I am dying of grief like one without a protector. O queen, while I live, this ocean of sorrow is hard for me to cross.
t.2.53.25: "How wretched it is that I, longing to see Rāghava together with Lakṣmaṇa, cannot find him here today!" Lamenting thus, the greatly illustrious king swiftly fell upon his bed in a swoon.
t.2.53.26: As the king lamented thus and sank into a swoon, the queen, Rāma's mother, heard his words, more piteous still and doubly grievous on account of Rāma, and was once again overcome with fear.
